structure.title: Acquiring and securing rule
structure.text: Early chapters distinguish kinds of principalities and the difficulties of gaining dependable military and political support.

structure.title: Conduct and circumstance
structure.text: Later chapters test familiar virtues against political outcomes, then return to fortune and Italy's predicament.

people.name: The new prince
people.text: A ruler who has just won power by force, luck or others' help, and must hold it without the habits of obedience a long-established family enjoys.

people.name: Virtù
people.text: Machiavelli's word for the boldness, skill and readiness to act that a ruler needs to master events, which has little to do with goodness.

people.name: Fortuna
people.text: Chance, which Machiavelli compares to a flooding river that controls half of what we do, and which a prepared ruler can dam in advance.

context.title: Effective conduct
context.text: Praiseworthy intentions and successful rule can diverge. Machiavelli examines that divergence without making every cruel act useful.
context.takeaway: Follow the claimed consequence of each recommendation.

context.title: An unstable Italy
context.text: Competing states and outside powers form the background to the examples. Dependence on another ruler's force is a recurring vulnerability.
context.takeaway: Independence requires means, not declarations alone.

notice.why: Machiavelli does not treat all forms of submission as equally secure.

notice.text: Watch historical examples resist neat rules.

opening: A ruler who keeps his promises may be destroyed by someone who does not. One who tries to be generous can end up taxing his people until they hate him. Machiavelli examines these predicaments with the attention of a man who has watched governments fall and lost his own position with one of them. His advice forces the question that respectable accounts of leadership often evade: what happens when the conduct that earns admiration is not the conduct that keeps you in power?
